title: Picking the strike
teaches: How to pick a strike for a chart view: deeper in the money costs more and moves more like the stock, further out is cheaper but needs a bigger move, break-even has to sit inside your target, and a put's strike works like a stop a gap can't jump.

sources.publisher: The Options Clearing Corporation and the US options exchanges

Same copy F6.03 cites.

facts.quote: For an option with a Delta of .50, an investor can expect about a $.50 move in that option’s premium given a $1 move, up or down, in the underlying.
facts.claim: A .50 delta option moves about 50 cents for each $1 the stock moves.

facts.quote: As the stock price rises and the call option goes deeper-in-the-money, Delta typically approaches 1.00 because of the increased likelihood the option will be in-the-money at expiration.
facts.claim: The deeper in the money a call goes, the closer its delta gets to 1.00.

facts.quote: The closer an option's Delta is to 1.00 or -1.00, the more the price of the option responds (in terms of dollars) to actual long or short stock when the underlying moves.
facts.claim: The closer delta is to 1.00 (or -1.00 for a put), the more the option moves like owning (or shorting) the stock.

facts.quote: Some traders view Delta as a percentage probability an option will wind up in-the-money at expiration. Therefore, an at-the-money option would have a .50 Delta or 50% chance of being in-the-money at expiration.
facts.claim: Some traders read delta as the rough odds an option finishes in the money; at the money that's about .50.

facts.quote: An option with less than a .10 Delta (or less than 10% probability of being in-the-money) is not viewed as very likely to be in-the-money at any point and will need a strong move
facts.claim: An option under a .10 delta is unlikely to finish in the money and needs a strong move to be worth anything.

facts.quote: As expiration nears, in-the-money call Deltas increase toward 1.00, at-the-money call Deltas remain around .50 and out-of-the-money call Deltas fall toward 0 provided other inputs remain constant.
facts.claim: Into expiry, in-the-money call deltas rise toward 1.00, at-the-money ones stay near .50, and out-of-the-money ones fall toward 0.

facts.quote: It is important to remember that Delta is constantly changing during market hours and will typically not accurately predict the exact change in an option’s premium.
facts.claim: Delta keeps changing, so it's a guide to the option's move, not an exact prediction.

facts.quote: The maximum loss is limited and occurs if the investor still holds the call at expiration and the stock is below the strike price.
facts.claim: A call held to expiry with the stock below the strike is the worst case: it expires worthless.

facts.quote: At expiration, the strategy breaks even if the stock price is equal to the strike price plus the initial cost of the call option.
facts.claim: A long call breaks even at expiry at the strike plus the premium paid.

facts.quote: The smaller initial outlay also gives the buyer a chance to achieve greater percentage gains (i.e., greater leverage).
facts.claim: Paying less up front gives a call buyer the chance at bigger percentage gains.

facts.quote: Generally speaking, the earlier and sharper the increase in the stock's value, the better for the long call strategy.
facts.claim: A long call does best when the stock rises early and sharply.

facts.quote: An option holder cannot lose more than the initial price paid for the option.
facts.claim: An option buyer can't lose more than the premium paid.

facts.quote: Once time value disappears, all that remains is intrinsic value. For in-the-money options, that is the difference between the stock price and the strike price.
facts.claim: At expiry a call is worth the stock price minus the strike, if it's in the money.

facts.quote: if a quick turnaround starts looking unlikely, it might make sense to sell the call while it still has some time value. A timely decision might allow the investor to recoup some or even all of the investment.
facts.claim: If the trade isn't working, selling the call while it still has time value can recover part of what you paid.

facts.quote: The investor buys a put contract that is compatible with the expected timing and size of a downturn.
facts.claim: A put buyer picks the contract to fit how big and how soon the expected drop is.

facts.quote: At expiration, the strategy breaks even if the stock price equals the strike price minus the cost of the option.
facts.claim: A long put breaks even at expiry at the strike minus the premium paid.

facts.quote: The worst that can happen is for the stock price to be above the strike price at expiration with the put owner still holding the position.
facts.claim: A put held to expiry with the stock above the strike is the worst case: it expires worthless.

facts.quote: Once time value disappears, all that remains is intrinsic value. For in-the-money options, that is the difference between the going stock price and the strike price.
facts.claim: At expiry a put is worth the strike minus the stock price, if it's in the money.

facts.quote: An option's premium (intrinsic value plus time value) generally increases as the option becomes further in-the-money. It decreases as the option becomes more deeply out-of-the-money.
facts.claim: The deeper in the money a strike, the more the option costs; the further out, the less.

facts.quote: Generally, as expiration approaches, the levels of an option's time value decrease or erode for both puts and calls. This effect is most noticeable with at-the-money options.
facts.claim: Time value erodes toward expiry, and at-the-money options feel it most.

facts.quote: This means an option buyer can pay a relatively small premium for market exposure in relation to the contract value (usually 100 shares of the underlying stock).
facts.claim: One stock option contract usually covers 100 shares, for a premium that's small next to the shares' value.

facts.quote: An investor can see large percentage gains from comparatively small, favorable percentage moves in the underlying product.
facts.claim: Small favorable moves in the stock can mean large percentage gains in the option.

facts.quote: If the underlying stock price does not rise or fall as anticipated during the lifetime of the option, leverage could magnify the investment's percentage loss.
facts.claim: If the move doesn't come before expiry, the option's percentage loss is magnified.

facts.quote: Options offer their owners a predetermined, set risk. However, if the owner's options expire with no value, this loss can be the entire amount of the premium paid for the option.
facts.claim: A buyer's risk is set at the premium, and an option that expires worthless loses all of it.

facts.quote: By definition, an at-the-money or out-of-the-money option has no intrinsic value.
facts.claim: At-the-money and out-of-the-money options have no intrinsic value.

facts.quote: The choice of strike prices determines where the downside protection 'kicks in’.
facts.claim: The put's strike sets where the protection starts.

facts.quote: The strike becomes the 'floor' exit price at which the investor can liquidate the stock, regardless of how low the market price might fall.
facts.claim: With a protective put, the strike is a floor price you can sell at, however low the stock falls.

facts.quote: If the purchase price of the stock was the same as the strike price of the option, then the loss is limited to the premium paid for the put option.
facts.claim: Stock bought at the strike: the worst loss is the put's premium.

facts.quote: If the stock's purchase price was higher (lower), then the loss would be greater (smaller) by exactly that amount.
facts.claim: Stock bought above the strike: add the gap between your cost and the strike to the worst loss.

facts.quote: The major drawback of the strategy is its cost, which raises the bar on netting upside profits.
facts.claim: The put's cost is the drawback: it raises the bar for profit.

facts.quote: The strike price sets the minimum exit price.
facts.claim: A protective put's strike is your minimum exit price.

facts.quote: many experts recommend that you designate an exit strategy or cut-off point in advance, and hold firm.
facts.claim: Set your exit or cut-off point before the trade, and stick to it.

facts.quote: The more an option is out of the money and the shorter the remaining time to expiration, the greater the risk that an option holder will lose all or part of his investment in the option.
facts.claim: The further out of the money and the less time left, the bigger the risk of losing the premium.

facts.quote: The greater the price movement of the underlying interest necessary for the option to become profitable (that is, the more the option is out of the money when purchased and the greater the cost of the option)
facts.claim: The further out of the money an option is when you buy it, the bigger the move it needs to turn a profit.

facts.quote: The table demonstrates how increased leverage results in greater profit potential on the upside and greater risk of loss on the downside.
facts.claim: More leverage means more profit potential if right and more risk of loss if wrong.

facts.quote: An option normally has very little time value if it is substantially in the money.
facts.claim: A deep in-the-money option usually carries very little time value.

facts.quote: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order.
facts.claim: A stop order's stop price is not a guaranteed fill price.

facts.quote: The execution price an investor receives for this market order can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the prices of available liquidity when the market order executes.
facts.claim: Once triggered, a stop becomes a market order that can fill well away from the stop price.

facts.quote: Picking your options strike price boils down to a couple of key decisions, such as: What price do you think the underlying stock will move to over a certain period of time
facts.claim: Picking a strike starts with where you think the stock is going and over what time.

facts.quote: Intuitively, the greater the probability suggested by delta, the more expensive the option will be.
facts.claim: The higher a strike's delta, the more the option costs.

facts.quote: You almost always want to look for options that are heavily traded and have small bid-ask spreads if you want to focus on reducing your trading costs.
facts.claim: Heavily traded options with small bid-ask spreads keep your trading costs down.

facts.quote: In-the-money options are relatively more expensive than out-of-the-money options.
facts.claim: In-the-money options cost more than out-of-the-money ones.

facts.quote: A delta of 0.70 also implies a 70% probability that the option will be in the money at expiration.
facts.claim: Fidelity reads a 0.70 delta as about a 70% chance of finishing in the money.

facts.quote: the maximum potential loss is the premium paid to purchase the call options.
facts.claim: A call buyer's most possible loss is the premium paid.

facts.quote: Of course, once you exercise the options, you have to pay for the stock at the strike price
facts.claim: The strike is what you pay per share if you exercise a call.

facts.quote: For example, if a long call is showing a delta of .30, the trader might think of the position as if he were long 30 shares.
facts.claim: A call's delta times 100 is roughly how many shares the contract acts like.

facts.quote: many traders look at delta as an approximate percentage chance that an option will be ITM at expiration. Although it's not a perfect science, an options delta calculation can provide a pretty close estimate.
facts.claim: Many traders use delta as approximate odds of finishing in the money; it's an estimate, not a certainty.

facts.quote: the 135-strike call is OTM, and its 0.22 delta implies it has about a 22% chance of finishing ITM at expiration. Another way of expressing this is to say the option has about a 78% chance of expiring worthless.
facts.claim: A 0.22 delta reads as about a 22% chance of finishing in the money, or about 78% of expiring worthless.

facts.quote: This doesn't mean higher-delta options are always profitable because option buyers have to contest with time decay
facts.claim: A high delta doesn't make a trade profitable; buyers still have to beat time decay.

facts.quote: At-the-money (ATM) options usually have a delta near 0.50.
facts.claim: An at-the-money call usually has a delta near 0.50.

facts.quote: Delta should increase (and approach 1.00) as the option gets deeper ITM.
facts.claim: A call's delta climbs toward 1.00 the deeper in the money it goes.

facts.quote: ATM options usually have a delta near –0.50.
facts.claim: An at-the-money put usually has a delta near -0.50.

facts.quote: Delta should decrease (and approach –1.00) as the option gets deeper ITM.
facts.claim: A put's delta heads toward -1.00 the deeper in the money it goes.

facts.quote: An at-the-money (ATM) call option typically has delta of around .50. Out-of-the-money (OTM) call options have delta less than .50, and in-the-money (ITM) call options have delta greater than .50.
facts.claim: Call deltas: about .50 at the money, below .50 out of the money, above .50 in the money.

facts.quote: Some stocks have more actively traded options than others, and there can be substantial differences in spreads between the bids and asks in the options market.
facts.claim: Bid-ask spreads can differ a lot from one option to another.

facts.quote: More liquid markets can make it easier to get in and out of stock and options positions at the desired prices.
facts.claim: Liquid options are easier to get in and out of at your price.

facts.quote: Many traders tend to look for spreads that are 10% or less of the ask price.
facts.claim: A common rule of thumb: a bid-ask spread of 10% of the ask or less.

facts.quote: if a put option has a strike price that is greater than the current market price of the underlying security, it is said to be in-the-money
facts.claim: A put is in the money when its strike is above the stock price.

facts.quote: If the stock stays strong, the investor still gets the benefit of upside gains.
facts.claim: A protective put leaves your upside open: if the stock rises, you keep the gains.

facts.quote: If it opens below $28, the order is triggered by the opening price and becomes a market sell order at whatever that prevailing price may be.
facts.claim: When a stock opens below a sell stop, the stop becomes a market order at whatever price is there.

facts.quote: Trade shares; options are only a defined-risk alternative.
facts.claim: Our rule: trade shares; an option is only a defined-risk alternative.

facts.quote: Options occasionally; no further rules. The premium paid is the stop.
facts.claim: Our rule: options only occasionally, and the premium paid is the stop.

walkthroughs.title: In, at or out of the money
steps: Same stock, same expiry. The deeper in the money the strike, the more you pay for it.
Deep in the money, a call's delta heads toward 1.00. It moves most like the stock. A put's heads to -1.00.
At the money, a call's delta sits near .50. Way out of the money, delta's small and you need a strong move.

walkthroughs.title: Let the chart pick the strike
steps: Start with the chart. Know the price you expect, and how soon you expect it.
Held to expiry, a call breaks even at strike plus premium. A put breaks even at strike minus premium.
If you'll hold to expiry, your target has to clear that line. If not, it's the wrong strike.
Further-out strikes are cheaper, but they need a bigger move. And the sooner it comes, the better.

walkthroughs.title: The strike and your stop
steps: Own the stock and a put, and the put's strike is your floor. You can sell there until it expires.
A stop is a trigger, not a promised fill. Gap below it and you sell at whatever's there.
A higher put strike puts the floor closer, and it costs more.
With a call you buy, the premium is the most you can lose. Your chart stop still tells you when you're wrong.

questions.q: The stock's at 100 and you're scanning the calls, all one expiry. Which strike costs you the most?
questions.why: The 90 call. It's the deepest in the money, so it's already worth something before the stock moves another cent. That built-in value is intrinsic value, the stock price minus the strike, and you pay for it. Same stock, same expiry: the deeper in the money, the more it costs. The further out, the cheaper. The 95 is in the money too, just not as deep. The 100 sits right at the money with no intrinsic value. The 110 is out of the money and the cheapest of the four. So a big premium on a deep strike isn't the market overcharging you. You're paying for value it already has.
questions.lesson_line: You pay for the value a strike already has. Deeper in costs more.

wrong.The 100 call: Right at the money it has no intrinsic value. The 90 has real value on top of its time value.
wrong.The 110 call: It's out of the money, so it's the cheapest of the four, not the priciest.
wrong.The 95 call: In the money, yes, but not as deep as the 90. The deeper the strike, the more you pay.

questions.simple: The 90 call, because it's the deepest in the money, and the deeper in a strike is, the more it costs.

questions.q: An at-the-money call usually has a delta near 0.50.
questions.why: True. At the money, delta sits near 0.50. Deep in the money it heads toward 1.00, and far out of the money it's small.
questions.lesson_line: Delta shows where a strike sits: near 1.00 deep in, near 0.50 at the money, small far out.

questions.q: You want a put that trades almost like shorting the stock, which sits at 80. Same expiry on all four. Which strike?
questions.why: The 90 put. A put is in the money when its strike sits above the stock, so the 90 is the deepest in of the four. That pushes its delta closest to -1.00. Delta is how much the option moves for each $1 the stock moves. Near -1.00, the put gains close to a dollar for every dollar the stock drops, which is what a short does. The 85 is in the money too, but less deep. The 80 sits at the money, around -0.50, so it moves about half as much. The 70 is out of the money and moves the least of the four. If you want short-like moves from a put, go deep in the money.
questions.lesson_line: For a put, deep in the money means a strike well above the stock. That's the one that trades like a short.

wrong.The 80 put: Right at the money its delta sits near -0.50. It moves about half as much as the stock, for now.
wrong.The 70 put: That's out of the money, struck under the stock. Its delta is the furthest of the four from -1.00.
wrong.The 85 put: In the money, yes, but not as deep as the 90. Its delta sits further from -1.00.

questions.simple: The 90 put. It's the deepest in the money, so it moves the most like being short the stock.

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: Buy further out of the money and the stock needs a ___ move before you profit.
questions.why: Bigger. The options disclosure document says an option bought further out of the money needs a greater move to become profitable. OIC adds that an option under a .10 delta needs a strong move. A smaller, slower or calmer move works against a far strike.
questions.lesson_line: Every step further out raises the bar the stock has to clear.
questions.simple: Bigger, because the further out of the money you buy, the more the stock has to move before you make money.

questions.q: You buy a call, at any strike. What's the most the trade can lose?
choices: Nothing, if it's in the money now
questions.why: The premium you paid. A call buyer can't lose more than that. A pricier strike just puts more dollars on the line.
questions.lesson_line: Whatever strike you pick, its premium is your worst case. Pick one you can afford to lose.

wrong.The strike price times 100: The strike is what you'd pay per share if you exercised. Your risk as a buyer is the premium.
wrong.Unlimited, if the stock collapses: A collapse leaves the call worthless at expiry, nothing more. A call buyer's loss stops at the premium.
wrong.Nothing, if it's in the money now: In the money today can be out of the money at expiry. The premium is still at risk.

questions.q: Own 100 shares and one 45 put, and you can sell at 45 however far the stock falls, until expiry.
questions.why: True. The put's strike is a floor exit price for the life of the put, however low the stock goes. One contract usually covers 100 shares.
questions.lesson_line: A put's strike is a floor under your shares, until expiry.

questions.q: To spend less, you move your call strike further out of the money. That cuts your risk of losing the whole premium.
questions.why: False. You spend fewer dollars, but the odds of losing all of them go up. The further out of the money you buy, the bigger the move the stock needs before the call pays anything. Less time left makes it worse. Cheaper isn't safer. It's a smaller check with a bigger chance of going to zero. If you want less money on the line, buy fewer contracts of a strike that fits your target. Don't reach for a strike the stock may never get to.
questions.lesson_line: If you want less at risk, buy fewer contracts, not a further strike.
questions.simple: False. A strike further out costs less, but it's more likely to expire worth nothing.

questions.q: A name you like is basing, and this time you want to use calls. Before you even open the chain, what do you settle?
choices: How much you'd like to make
questions.why: Where you think it's going, and how soon. That's your chart's job, and it picks the strike for you. A target tells you how far in or out you can go. A timeframe tells you which expiry gives the move room to show up. Cost and volume come after that. The cheapest strike is the furthest out, and it needs the biggest move. A busy strike only matters among the ones that already fit your view. And the money you'd like to make doesn't move the stock at all.
questions.lesson_line: Your chart picks the strike. Price and volume come after.

wrong.Which strike is cheapest today: The cheapest strike is the furthest out, and it needs the biggest move. Price comes after the view.
wrong.Which strike traded most today: Liquidity matters, but only among the strikes that fit your target and timing.
wrong.How much you'd like to make: What you want to make doesn't move the stock. The chart's view comes first.

questions.simple: Your target and your timing, because the strike has to fit the move you expect.

reasons: fixed before (leading stem reworded by the checker)

questions.q: Stock at 50, and you pick up the 52.50 call for 0.99. If you hold it to expiry, where does the stock need to be to break even?
questions.why: $53.49. Strike plus what you paid: 52.50 plus 0.99 is 53.49. At expiry a call is only worth the stock minus the strike. So the stock has to clear 52.50 by the full 0.99 just to hand your money back. Anywhere between 52.50 and 53.49, the call is in the money and you're still losing. Before expiry the call still holds some time value, so you can sell it early for more than it's worth at expiry. But if you plan to hold, your target has to sit above 53.49 or the trade doesn't make sense.
questions.lesson_line: Strike plus premium is the line. If your target doesn't clear it, pick another strike.
questions.simple: $53.49, because a call held to expiry breaks even at the strike plus what you paid for it.

wrong.$51.51: That takes the premium off the strike, which is how a put breaks even.
wrong.$52.50: That's just the strike. You still have to earn back the 0.99 you paid.
wrong.$50.99: That adds the premium to today's price. It goes on the strike.

questions.q: Your chain shows a call with a 0.22 delta. Read as rough odds, how likely is it to expire worthless?
questions.why: About 78%. Plenty of traders read delta as rough odds of finishing in the money. A 0.22 delta says about a 22% shot. Take 0.22 from one and you get 0.78, so about 78% that it expires worthless. Treat that as a rough read, not a promise. Delta changes all day as the stock moves. And finishing in the money isn't the same as making money. Held to expiry, you need the stock past the strike plus what you paid, so your odds of a profit are lower still. A 0.22 delta is a long shot. Know that going in.
questions.lesson_line: Delta is rough odds of finishing in the money. Rough, and it says nothing about profit.
questions.simple: About 78%, since a 0.22 delta reads as roughly a 22% chance of finishing in the money.

deeper.trap: In the money is not the same as profit. The 22% is the rough chance the call finishes in the money at all. Held to expiry, a profit needs the stock past the strike plus the premium, which is a higher bar. Schwab warns that a higher delta does not make a trade profitable.

wrong.22%: That's the rough chance it finishes in the money. Flip it for the chance it expires worthless.
wrong.2.2%: Slipped a decimal on the 0.22 delta.
wrong.99.78%: Took 0.22 off 100 without turning the delta into a percent first.

questions.story: You've got two call strikes that both fit your chart, each around 2.00. One trades all day with a 0.05 spread. The other is 0.60 wide and barely trades.
questions.q: Which one are you buying?
choices: The wide one, it may be a bargain
Both work, I'll get the mid price
questions.why: The busy, tight one. The spread is the gap between the bid and the ask, and you pay it twice: once going in, once coming out. On a 2.00 option, 0.05 is a small toll. A 0.60 spread is a big chunk of the price gone before the stock moves at all. A thin market also makes it harder to get out at your price right when you need to. When two strikes fit the chart equally, let liquidity break the tie.
questions.lesson_line: When two strikes fit, take the one you can get in and out of cleanly.

wrong.The wide one, it may be a bargain: A wide, quiet market makes it harder to get in and out at your price. That's a cost, not a bargain.
wrong.Either, spreads don't change much: Spreads can differ a lot from one option to the next, and a wide one is a real cost.
wrong.Both work, I'll get the mid price: In a thin, wide market the mid is a hope, not a fill. Busy, tight options keep that cost down.

questions.simple: The busy, tight one, because you pay the spread going in and coming out, and a small one costs you less.

reasons: fixed before (option prices added to the story)

questions.q: A call has a 0.70 delta. One contract covers 100 shares. Roughly how many shares does it act like, for now?
questions.why: About 70. Delta times the 100 shares a contract covers. Delta keeps changing as the stock moves, so it's a snapshot.
questions.lesson_line: Pick the strike for the share-like exposure you want: delta times 100 per contract.

questions.story: The stock's at 100 and your chart says 108 by expiry. The 95 call is 7.10, the 100 call 4.15, the 105 call 2.20 and the 110 call 1.00.
questions.q: Expiry day, it closes right at 108. Which call is a total loss?
questions.why: The 110 call. You nailed the target and still lost all 1.00. The stock never got to 110, so that call expires worth nothing. The other three finish in the money. The 95 is worth 108 minus 95, the 100 is worth 108 minus 100, and the 105 is worth 108 minus 105. Each one beats what it cost. That's the trap with a strike above your target. It looks cheap, but your own target can't pay it. Pick the strike from your target, not from the price tag.
questions.lesson_line: A strike above your target can't pay at expiry, even when you're right.

wrong.The 95 call: At 108 it's worth 108 minus 95, well above the 7.10 you paid.
wrong.The 100 call: At 108 it's worth 108 minus 100, above the 4.15 you paid.
wrong.The 105 call: At 108 it's worth 108 minus 105, more than the 2.20 you paid.

questions.simple: The 110 call, because the stock ended under its strike, so it expired worth nothing even though you were right.

questions.story: The stock's at 100. The 95 call costs 7.10, the 100 call 4.15 and the 110 call 1.00. On expiry day it closes at 115.
questions.q: You took the 110 call. What did it make, in percent?
questions.why: Up 400%. At 115 the 110 call is worth 115 minus 110, so 5. Take off the 1.00 you paid and you're up 4. 4 on a 1.00 outlay is 400%. The stock itself moved 15%. That's what a small outlay buys you, a big percent on a modest move. But it only worked because the move came in time. Close at 110 on expiry day and that same call is a 100% loss. That's the deal with far strikes.
questions.lesson_line: Far strikes pay the biggest percent, but only when the big move shows up in time.

wrong.Up 500%: That's the call's value against its cost. Take the 1.00 you paid off first.
wrong.Up 15%: That's the stock's move. The option's percent runs far bigger on the same move.
wrong.Up 1,400%: That counts the whole run from 100. The call only gains above its 110 strike.

questions.simple: Up 400%, because you measure the gain against the 1.00 you paid, not against the stock's move.

deeper.trap: The big percent needs the big move to come before expiry. If it doesn't come in time, the call can expire worthless and lose all you paid. More leverage means more profit if you're right and more risk of loss if you're wrong.

questions.story: The stock's at 100. The 90 call costs 10.95 and the 110 call costs 1.00. Both expire in a month.
questions.q: Hold both to expiry. Which one breaks even closer to where the stock trades now?
questions.why: The 90 call, at 100.95. Strike plus premium: 90 plus 10.95. That's barely above today's 100. The 110 call needs the stock past 110 plus the 1.00 you paid, a real rally just to get back to flat. The gap is what you're paying for. Most of the 90 call's price is value it already has, because it's already in the money. Very little of it is time value. So you put more cash up front, but you need far less of a move. Cheap and close are two different things.
questions.lesson_line: Deep in the money costs more cash, but its break-even sits close.

wrong.The 110 call, at 101: That adds the premium to today's price. Break-even is strike plus premium, 110 plus 1.00.
wrong.Both, at their strikes: The strike alone isn't enough. You have to earn back the premium on top of it.
wrong.The 110 call, at 109: That takes the premium off, which is the put rule. A call breaks even at strike plus premium.

questions.simple: The 90 call, because most of its price is value it already has, so strike plus premium lands near today's price.

deeper.trap: Cheaper does not mean a lower bar. The 110 call costs only 1.00, yet held to expiry it needs the stock above 110 plus 1.00. The 90 call costs 10.95, but most of that is value it already has, so its line sits just above today's price. The catch is the cash: the 90 call puts far more dollars at risk.

questions.story: ZQRT trades at 80 and your chart says it breaks down to 72 within a month. The 75 put costs 1.50 and the 70 put costs 0.50.
questions.q: You grab the 75 put. ZQRT closes at 72 on expiry day. What did you make or lose per contract?
questions.why: Made $150. At 72 the 75 put is worth 75 minus 72, which is 3. Take off the 1.50 you paid and you keep 1.50 a share. One contract covers 100 shares, so that's $150. The put only gains under its 75 strike, so the drop from 80 down to 75 earned you nothing. The cheaper 70 put was struck under your 72 target, so it expired worthless. Same idea as with calls: put the strike where your target can pay it.
questions.lesson_line: Put the strike where your target can pay it, with room for the premium.

wrong.Made $300: That's what the put is worth, 75 minus 72, times 100 shares. Take off the 1.50 you paid.
wrong.Made $650: That counts the whole drop from 80. The put only gains under its 75 strike.
wrong.Lost $150: The put finished in the money, worth more than the 1.50 it cost.

questions.simple: Made $150. The put ended worth 75 minus 72, you paid 1.50, and one contract covers a hundred shares.

questions.q: If the stock just sits, an out-of-the-money call's delta tends to drift toward 0 as expiry nears.
questions.why: True. With other inputs steady, out-of-the-money call deltas fall toward 0 as expiry approaches. The call reacts less and less.
questions.lesson_line: An out-of-the-money strike wants its move early and sharp.

questions.q: A call with a 0.70 delta has about a 70% chance of making you money.
questions.why: False. Read loosely, delta is rough odds of finishing in the money. Held to expiry, profit needs more: the stock past strike plus premium.
questions.lesson_line: In the money and in profit are two different finish lines.

questions.story: You're swinging a stock for about two weeks and want to use options this time. You want something that tracks the shares closely and doesn't bleed much to time.
questions.q: Which strike fits that plan?
choices: A call right at the money
questions.why: A deep in-the-money call. Its delta runs toward 1.00, so it moves almost dollar for dollar with the stock. Very little of its price is time value, so there's not much to bleed while you wait. The catch is cost. It's the priciest strike on the chain, so more cash rides on the trade. At the money, delta sits near .50 and time decay bites hardest. Out of the money, the whole price is time value. If you want stock-like behavior from an option, you pay for it up front.
questions.lesson_line: Deep in the money gets you stock-like moves and little decay. You pay up front for it.

wrong.A far out-of-the-money call: It has no intrinsic value, so its whole price is time value, and its delta is small.
wrong.A call right at the money: Its delta sits near 0.50, and time decay hits at-the-money options hardest.
wrong.A strike at your target: With your target above today's price, that strike is out of the money. Its whole price is time value.

questions.simple: A deep in-the-money call, because it moves almost like the stock and little of its price can melt away.

deeper.trap: Stock-like works both ways. With delta near 1.00, the call falls almost as fast as the stock when the stock falls. It also costs the most of any strike, so more dollars ride on the trade. You keep the buyer's cap: you can't lose more than the premium you paid.

questions.q: You own shares from 50 and buy the 45 put for 0.55 as insurance. Held to expiry, what's the most you can lose per share?
questions.why: $5.55 a share. The put lets you sell at 45 no matter how far the stock drops. So you can lose the stretch from 50 down to 45, plus the 0.55 the put cost. 50 minus 45 is 5, plus 0.55 is 5.55. Had you bought the shares right at 45, you'd only be risking the premium. Every dollar you paid above the strike adds to the worst case. And the floor only lasts until the put expires. After that you're holding plain stock again.
questions.lesson_line: With a put under your shares, the worst case is cost minus strike, plus what the put cost.
questions.simple: $5.55, because the put lets you sell at 45, so you lose 50 minus 45 plus the 0.55 it cost.

deeper.trap: The floor ends when the put expires. After that you own plain stock again, with nothing under it. And the 0.55 is spent whether the stock falls or not, which raises the bar for profit on the way up.

wrong.$50.55: Added the premium to your 50 cost and forgot the strike.

questions.q: Your sell stop sits at 45. Bad news hits overnight and the stock opens at 38. Your shares still sell at 45.
questions.why: False. A stop is a trigger, not a price promise. When the stock opens at 38, your stop fires and turns into a market order. It sells at whatever's there, down around 38, not 45. Gaps jump right over stops. That's why a tight stop never licenses a monster position. A 45 put is different. It lets you sell at 45 however low the stock opens, until the put expires. You pay a premium for that floor.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger. A put's strike is a floor. Know which one you're holding.
questions.simple: False, because a stop only starts a market sale, and after a gap down it fills wherever the stock opens.

deeper.counter: The put's floor has a price. You pay the premium up front, and that cost raises your bar for profit. It also protects only until the put expires. A stop promises no price at all.

questions.story: You own shares from 50, still sitting at 50. Two months out, the 47.50 put costs 1.20 and the 45 put costs 0.55.
questions.q: Which put gives you the closer floor, and what's the catch?
choices: The 45 put, and it's cheaper too
The 47.50 put, but it costs more
The 47.50 put, but it caps your upside
The 47.50 put, but you have to sell
questions.answer: The 47.50 put, but it costs more
questions.why: The 47.50 put, but you pay more for it. The strike is where your protection starts, so 47.50 catches you sooner than 45. It costs 1.20 against 0.55. That 1.20 is spent whether the stock falls or not, so it raises your bar for profit. Your upside stays open with either put, less what you paid. So it's a trade-off, a closer floor or a cheaper one. I'd start from the chart, at the level where you'd want out anyway. Then see what that floor costs.
questions.lesson_line: The closer the floor, the more you pay for it.

wrong.The 45 put, and it's cheaper too: Cheaper, yes, but its floor sits lower, so more of any drop is yours.
wrong.The 47.50 put, but it caps your upside: A put leaves your upside open. If the stock runs, you keep the gains, less what the put cost.
wrong.The 47.50 put, but you have to sell: The strike is a floor you can sell at, not a duty to sell. If the stock holds up, you keep the shares.

questions.simple: The 47.50 put protects closer to your price, but it costs more, and that cost raises the bar for profit.

deeper.trap: A put is a floor, not a ceiling. If the stock stays strong, you keep the upside, less what the put cost. The closer floor costs more, so it takes a bigger bite of that upside.

questions.story: You bought a 105 call when the stock broke out at 100. Your plan says the trade is wrong below 96. Today it closes at 95.
questions.q: What do you do with the call?
choices: Hold, the most you lose is the premium
Sell it on a bounce back to 100
questions.why: Sell it, it closed below 96. Your plan set the cut-off at 96 before the trade. OIC says to set an exit in advance and hold firm. Selling while the call still has time value can recover part of what you paid. Held to expiry below the strike, it can lose the whole premium.
questions.lesson_line: The option caps your loss. Your chart stop still decides when you're wrong.

wrong.Hold, the most you lose is the premium: The cap is real, but your plan said out below 96. Hold a broken trade to expiry and you can lose the whole premium.
wrong.Buy more, it's cheaper now: It's cheaper because the trade is going against you. Adding breaks the plan you set in advance.
wrong.Sell it on a bounce back to 100: Waiting for a better price breaks the exit you set in advance. And time value keeps eroding while you wait.

questions.simple: Sell it, because your plan said the trade is wrong below 96, and selling now saves part of what you paid.

reasons: rests on a rule the owner's rulebook speaks to (B25: premium paid is the stop)
fixed before (key reworded by the checker)

questions.q: A cheap far-out call is quoted 0.10 bid, 0.20 ask. How wide is that spread as a percent of the ask?
questions.why: 50%. The spread is 0.20 minus 0.10, so 0.10. Divide by the 0.20 ask and you get 0.5, half the price. Buy at 0.20, sell right back at 0.10, and half your money's gone before the stock does a thing. A common rule of thumb is a spread of 10% of the ask or less. This one's way past it. So check the spread before you click buy on a cheap far strike.
questions.lesson_line: On a cheap far strike, check the spread first. Half the price can vanish on the round trip.
questions.simple: 50%, because the gap between the 0.10 bid and the 0.20 ask is half the ask.

deeper.example: Buy at the 0.20 ask, then sell right back at the 0.10 bid. Half of what you paid is gone before the stock moves at all. Heavily traded options with small spreads keep that cost down.

reasons: fixed before (lesson line no longer contradicts q08)

wrong.100%: Divided the spread by the 0.10 bid instead of the ask.
wrong.67%: Divided the spread by the midpoint, not the ask.
wrong.10%: Read the 0.10 spread in dollars as 10 percent.

questions.story: The stock's at 40 with a week to expiry. The 45 call is offered at 0.03, with a 0.03 delta. A buddy calls it a cheap bet on a pop.
questions.q: What's your honest read on that call?
choices: Cheap, so the risk is small
Buy a lot, one pop pays for all
It moves like the stock, for less
It needs a big move in days
questions.answer: It needs a big move in days
questions.why: It needs a big move in days. A 0.03 delta reads as almost no chance of finishing in the money. Anything under a .10 delta needs a strong move just to be worth something. And the further out and the less time left, the likelier you lose the whole premium. Here you've got both. Cheap isn't low risk. You can lose all of it, and the odds say you will. Buying a pile of them doesn't change the odds. It just puts more money on the same long shot. I'd pass.
questions.lesson_line: Pennies on a far strike with days left is a long shot, not a bargain.

wrong.Cheap, so the risk is small: The price is small, but you can lose all of it, and the odds favor that.
wrong.Buy a lot, one pop pays for all: If the pop doesn't come in time, every contract can go to zero. A week isn't much time.
wrong.It moves like the stock, for less: A 0.03 delta barely reacts to the stock. Stock-like moves need a delta near 1.00.

questions.simple: It needs a big move in a few days, because a 0.03 delta with a week left is very unlikely to pay.

deeper.trap: Cheap is not the same as low risk. An option buyer's risk is the whole premium, and here the odds favor losing it. Buying many contracts doesn't change those odds. It only puts more dollars on the same long shot.

questions.q: Your chart says 110 by expiry, so you buy the 110 call for 1.00. Held to expiry, how far past 110 must it go to break even?
questions.why: $1.00 past it. Break-even is strike plus premium: 110 plus 1.00 is 111. Take off your 110 target and the stock has to beat it by 1. So if you're exactly right and it closes at 110, the call is at the money, worth nothing, and you lose it all. A strike at your target feels natural. Held to expiry, it can't pay at the target. Pick a strike whose break-even sits under your target. Or plan to sell before expiry, while the call still has time value.
questions.lesson_line: Held to expiry, a strike at your target loses even when you're right.
questions.simple: $1.00, because break-even is the strike plus the 1.00 you paid, and that sits above your 110 target.

deeper.trap: A strike at your target feels natural, but held to expiry it can't win at the target. The stock has to clear 110 plus 1.00. Pick a strike whose break-even sits below your target. Or plan to sell before expiry, while the call still has time value.

wrong.$100.00: Mixed up the dollars on a whole contract with the price per share.
wrong.$10.00: Slipped a decimal place on the 1.00 premium.
wrong.$111.00: That's the break-even itself. Take your 110 target off it.

questions.q: You buy the 50 put for 2.00. Held to expiry, the trade breaks even with the stock at 48.
questions.why: True. A put breaks even at the strike minus what you paid: 50 minus 2.00 is 48. Below 48 you're making money. Between 48 and 50 the put is in the money, but you're still losing part of the 2.00. At 50 or above it expires worthless. So if your downside target doesn't get under 48, that strike doesn't work as a hold to expiry.
questions.lesson_line: A put's break-even is the strike minus what you paid. Your target has to get below it.
questions.simple: True, because a put breaks even at the strike minus the premium, and 50 minus 2.00 is 48.

reasons: key rests on one cited fact (f16)

questions.q: Into the final weeks before expiry, time decay eats an at-the-money call harder than a deep in-the-money one.
questions.why: True. Every option loses time value as expiry gets closer, puts and calls alike. It shows most at the money. A deep in-the-money option has very little time value left to lose, since most of its price is real value. So if you're holding an at-the-money option into the last stretch, the clock works hardest against you. Either the move comes soon, or think about selling while some time value is left.
questions.lesson_line: Hold at the money into expiry and the clock works hardest against you.
questions.simple: True, because time value fades for every option near expiry, and at the money is where it shows most.

reasons: key rests on one cited fact (f20)

questions.q: A setup triggers on a stock you like. At UCT, the default play is calls, with shares as the backup.
questions.why: False. We trade shares. That's the default. Options are an occasional defined-risk alternative, not the plan. When we do use one, the premium paid is the stop. Go in assuming you can lose all of it. Shares keep it simple. No time decay, no strike to get wrong, and your stop sits where the chart says you're wrong. So treat everything in this lesson as a tool you reach for now and then, not the main way we trade.
questions.lesson_line: We trade shares. An option is the occasional defined-risk play, and its premium is the stop.
questions.simple: False, because we trade shares and only use options now and then, as a defined-risk choice.

conflicts: How firmly delta reads as a probability: Fidelity (f43) says a 0.70 delta 'implies a 70% probability' of finishing in the money, flatly; OIC (f4) frames it as how 'some traders view Delta', and Schwab (f47) says it is 'not a perfect science'. The file only ever asks it as rough odds (q10 'Read as rough odds', q18) and keys nothing on it being exact.

What delta's probability is a probability OF: Fidelity's 'The power of delta' page (s12) is subtitled as helping to 'assess the probability of making a profit', while OIC (f4) and Schwab (f47, f48) tie delta to finishing in the money at expiry, and Schwab (f49) warns higher delta does not mean profit. q18 keys the OIC / Schwab reading (in the money is not profit, break-even per OIC f9) and cites no Fidelity line for profit odds.

The disclosure document (f34) lists 'the greater the cost of the option' alongside 'the more the option is out of the money' as raising the move needed to profit, while q15 shows the costlier deep in-the-money call breaking even closer to the stock price. Not a contradiction: the ODD's cost point compares options at the same moneyness; a deep in-the-money call's extra cost is intrinsic value, and very little of it is time value (f36). q15's why and lesson say exactly that.
